intro: A keyboard sonata built from repeated attacks, changes of register and chords containing notes that refuse to agree. Its two repeated halves give Scarlatti room to make the same disturbances lead towards different keys.
question: How do repeated passages lead towards different harmonic destinations?

relations.label: The first half repeats
relations.basis: The sonata has two repeated halves; the first moves from D towards A. The measured pair falls inside that first half and its repeat, marked near 68 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.967, sustained 48.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 65.5 s (cache/form/scarlatti-sonata-k119.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The second half repeats
relations.basis: The second half returns towards D and is repeated near 204 s. These excerpts compare its later phrases, not the first half or a later Classical sonata-form recapitulation. CENS diagonal mean 0.941, sustained 42.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 72 s (cache/form/scarlatti-sonata-k119.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Remember a gesture, not every note
cues.text: Choose one short figure from the opening and keep its shape in mind. Repetition gives you another chance to recognise it; the interesting question is whether a familiar gesture leads towards the same destination.
cues.evidence: This is a listening prompt about repetition. The manuscript shows recurring short keyboard figures; it does not supply timings for Meyer’s performance: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Scarlatti,_Sonate_K._119_-_ms._Venise_XV,22.jpg
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Single lines and crowded chords
cues.text: Listen for the difference between a line moving through separate notes and a chord presenting several at once. The sonata’s crowded harmonies make the impact of an attack part of the musical argument.
cues.evidence: The Venice manuscript excerpt shows running figures beside increasingly full chords. This cue concerns that recurring contrast, not an exact chord at this timestamp: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Scarlatti,_Sonate_K._119_-_ms._Venise_XV,22.jpg
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A second hearing
cues.text: Compare this stretch with the opening. Try anticipating a gap, a change of register or a renewed burst of activity; repetition makes such interruptions recognisable rather than accidental.
cues.evidence: The recorded level and attack patterns after about 1:08 resemble the earlier passage, including a quieter gap followed by renewed activity. This suggests recurrence but is not a note-by-note repeat alignment.

cues.title: Following a royal pupil
cues.text: Scarlatti entered Portuguese royal service in 1719. In 1729 he followed his pupil Maria Bárbara to Spain after her marriage to the Spanish crown prince, continuing as her music master.
cues.evidence: The biographical chronology gives the move to Lisbon in 1719 and the continuation of his service in Spain from 1729: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenico_Scarlatti

cues.title: A familiar shape can go elsewhere
cues.text: Listen for gestures that resemble the earlier material but seem less settled in their surroundings. Follow the bass as well as the top line: a different support can change where a familiar figure appears to be heading.
cues.evidence: This is a question about harmonic direction, not a claim that the analysis has identified a particular chord or modulation. The second-half placement on the section map remains approximate.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Force without more attacks
cues.text: As the sound gains weight, distinguish stronger attacks from more frequent ones. A phrase can intensify while its basic rate of activity stays much the same.
cues.evidence: The measured level rises across roughly 2:45–3:00 while the detected attack rate changes relatively little. No tempo or expressive intention is inferred from that measurement.

cues.title: A copy, not a composition date
cues.text: K. 119 appears as number 22 in the Venice manuscript volume dated 1749. That dates this source, not necessarily the composition: the sonata may have existed before the surviving copy was made.
cues.evidence: IMSLP’s manuscript catalogue lists K. 119 in the 1749 group and explains that this volume is called XV in Kirkpatrick’s and Longo’s citations: https://imslp.org/wiki/Manuscript_Collection_of_Harpsichord_Sonatas%2C_I-Vnm_Mss.It.IV.199-213_(Scarlatti%2C_Domenico)

cues.title: Recognising the route back
cues.text: On this later hearing, follow the points where a phrase appears to settle. Do the returning figures feel different because you can now anticipate how they will finish?
cues.evidence: A repeat-oriented listening question, placed within the later recurring passage. Neither the exact repeat boundary nor the listener’s sense of resolution is established by the feature report.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: From attacks to resonance
cues.text: Follow the final phrase into the sound left behind by its last notes. Compare that spacing with the busy attacks earlier in the sonata.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows fewer attacks across the last phrase and very little remaining recorded sound near the end. It does not identify the exact final chord or infer a deliberate pedalling choice.

transitions.title: A cadence becomes a springboard back to D
transitions.how: The first half has travelled from D major to an A-major cadence. Taking the repeat now places the opening D-major material directly after that dominant-key ending. There is no specially composed bridge: the repeat sign makes the join, and the shared A lets a completed destination become the home key’s dominant in retrospect. The piano resumes the opening’s compact gestures and changes of register at the same quick pace, giving the ear a second chance to follow how the crowded chords are reached.
transitions.evidence: The approximate first-half-repeat marker is 1:08, a measured boundary between A-major and D-major regions. The provisional relation matches 0:17.5–1:06 with 1:23–2:11.5. The binary score supplies the D-to-A first-half route and repeat sign; the onset remains approximate despite the strong long-range recurrence.

transitions.title: The dominant becomes a point of departure
transitions.how: After the repeated A-major close, the second half begins from the dominant region rather than jumping straight to D. Familiar keyboard gestures are given less settled harmonic surroundings: changes in the bass redirect short figures while repeated attacks and dissonant chord notes keep the surface active. The eventual task is to bring closing material previously heard in A into D major. This is the second half of a binary design, not a miniature sonata-form development followed by a complete reprise.
transitions.evidence: The second-half marker is approximately 2:12, also a measured change after A-centred windows. Subsequent harmonic and level changes support a new span but do not identify every bass note. The score supplies the binary layout, dominant-region departure and tonic-directed closing material; the form relations support the two repeated halves.

transitions.title: The home cadence opens the route again
transitions.how: The second half reaches a D-major cadence, then its repeat sends the music back to the A-centred departure point. The harmonic route is reopened by a written repeat, not a new modulatory passage. The busy upper figures and their changing bass supports recur, so material that seemed exploratory can now be anticipated. On the piano, keep the bass destinations separate from the impact of the dissonant chords: the same disturbances must again be brought home to D.
transitions.evidence: The second-half-repeat boundary is approximately 3:24; a measured change occurs nearby at 3:28, with D-centred sound giving way to A-centred sound. The provisional relation matches 2:36.5–3:19 with 3:48.5–4:31. The score supplies the repeat and D-to-A restart; the section timestamp is retained as a passage estimate.

transitions.title: The crowded chords acquire a final destination
transitions.how: The second half’s later material brings its disruptions into D major. Chordal attacks and running figures may recall the first half’s close, but their bass now prepares A as the dominant of D rather than an A-major final destination. The last phrases reduce the need for fresh registers and harmonic excursions, and the A-to-D cadence settles the accumulated dissonance. Scarlatti closes with recognisable material redirected home, not with an unrelated concluding tune.
transitions.evidence: The approximate closing-passage marker is 4:18, a measured boundary. D-centred sound is sustained through the later passage, followed by fewer detected attacks and the terminal decay. The score supplies tonic-directed cadential material and the A-to-D close; the relation study matches this passage to the first traversal of the second half, not directly to the first half’s transposed cadence.

facts: Son of the opera composer Alessandro Scarlatti; born in the same year as Bach and Handel
Naples and Rome; Portuguese royal service from 1719; followed Maria Bárbara to Spain in 1729
555 keyboard sonatas in Ralph Kirkpatrick’s catalogue; earlier operas, cantatas and sacred music
composer.background:
Domenico Scarlatti was born in Naples, the sixth child of Alessandro Scarlatti, an established composer of opera and sacred music. He entered professional musical life as a teenager, working as an organist and composing for the stage. Domenico eventually concentrated on keyboard music in courts far from Naples, taking a different path from his father’s large operatic career. His first decades included church appointments, singers, theatrical commissions and the practical education of a musician expected to supply whatever his employer required.

In Rome he worked for the exiled Polish queen Maria Casimira and at St Peter’s, writing both opera and sacred music. The ten-part Stabat Mater, usually associated with these Roman years, combines four soprano lines with pairs of altos, tenors and basses. Its voices enter in changing combinations, and the density of the counterpoint can contract around a particular text.
composer.epithet: An Italian court musician in Lisbon and Madrid who made keyboard sonatas out of hand crossings, repeated notes and abrupt changes of harmonic ground.
